title: Birth: preparing for labour, choices and changes of plan
intro: Birth involves physical changes, decisions and support for both the person giving birth and the baby. Labour does not follow an identical timetable for everyone. Planning can make communication easier, while leaving room for changes when health or preferences change. This overview explains what to discuss with your maternity team; it does not replace an individual birth plan or instructions for an urgent situation.

sections.heading: Prepare preferences and a practical route to care
paragraphs: Discuss where birth is planned, who will support you, communication needs and what matters most to you. The appropriate setting depends on pregnancy circumstances, available services and transfer arrangements, not only personal preference. Ask how to reach maternity advice at any time and how you will travel. Mention previous birth experiences, trauma, medical conditions and any concerns about examinations or touch. A written plan records preferences rather than a promise that one exact sequence will happen. You can ask questions or change preferences as labour develops.

sections.heading: Contact the team about early labour and warning signs
paragraphs: Contractions may gradually become stronger and more regular, while early labour can stop and start. Follow your own team's advice about when to attend rather than using a universal contraction rule. Contact maternity care when waters break, including before contractions begin, and report the time, colour and smell. Reduced baby movements, vaginal bleeding, green or brown fluid, fever, severe persistent pain or possible labour before term need urgent maternity advice. Heavy bleeding, collapse, seizures or severe breathing difficulty requires emergency help. Do not wait for a contraction timer to confirm a problem.

sections.heading: Understand stages, examinations and monitoring
paragraphs: Labour usually includes opening of the cervix, birth of the baby and delivery of the placenta. The team assesses progress and the wellbeing of parent and baby, using observations and fetal heart monitoring suited to the circumstances. Ask what an examination or monitoring method is for, what it can show and what alternatives are reasonable. Consent, privacy and explanation remain important during labour. Slow progress or an unusual monitor finding needs interpretation with the whole clinical picture; a single number does not describe every person's labour or determine every decision.

sections.heading: Discuss comfort, pain relief and possible interventions
paragraphs: Movement, position changes, breathing, supportive kontaktor water may help when appropriate. Medicines and an epidural are other options, with benefits, limitations and side effects to discuss. Availability depends on the setting and your clinical circumstances; asking for pain relief is not failure. Induction, medicines to strengthen contractions, assisted vaginal birth or a caesarean may be proposed for particular reasons. Ask why, how urgent the decision is, the main risks and benefits and what alternatives exist. In an emergency explanations may be shorter, but the team should keep you informed and provide a chance to discuss events afterwards.

sections.heading: Include the first hours after birth and emotional support
paragraphs: After birth the team checks the baby and the parent's bleeding, placenta and any injuries. Ask about skin-to-skin contact and feeding support when clinically safe, as well as medicines or procedures recommended for either of you. If extra care separates parent and baby, ask how information and contact will be maintained. Before going home, confirm follow-up and warning signs. A difficult or unexpected birth can bring mixed feelings even when everyone is medically stable. Request a review of what happened and support for persistent distress rather than feeling you must simply be grateful and stay silent.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: changing a pain-relief preference
examples.text: Someone planned to use breathing and movement but later wants to discuss an epidural. They tell the midwife, ask about suitability and the available options, and update their preferences. The earlier written plan is not treated as a promise to refuse pain relief.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: waters before contractions
examples.text: A person's waters break before contractions are established. They call the maternity service, report the fluid and baby's movements and follow the individual assessment plan. They do not wait for strong contractions if the team advises assessment sooner.

questions: Which birth setting and support arrangements fit my pregnancy, and how do I contact care urgently?
What monitoring, pain relief or interventions might be proposed, and how will decisions be explained?
What checks and support will parent and baby need after birth, including a discussion of unexpected events?
